title: How great thou art
hookLine: a Swedish poem that traveled from language to language into English

lines: O STORE GUD: O GREAT GOD.
cards: A summer afternoon on the coast of Sweden. A storm rolls in fast over the water: dark sky, lightning, thunder loud enough to shake the windows. Then, just as fast, it's gone.
The air is washed clean. Birds start up again in the trees. Across the bay, church bells are ringing.
That, the story goes, is what a Swedish poet named Carl Boberg saw and heard on his walk home. He went in and wrote a poem. It began, in Swedish, O store Gud: O great God.

teach.b: Boberg's poem didn't stay in Sweden. It was set to a Swedish folk tune, and then it traveled.
Tradition says it passed into German, and then Russian, before an English missionary heard it sung in Ukraine and made the English hymn now known as How Great Thou Art.
The English words are modern and still under copyright, so they aren't sung here. But the hymn's bones are very old, and they're in the Bible. The poem moves the way the eighth Psalm moves.
In the King James Bible: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" First the sky, huge.
Then the small question: what are we, that you'd even notice? The hymn does the same.
It sees the stars, hears the thunder, walks through the woods among the birds, and only then turns to the cross and to Christ coming home.
Wonder first, then gratitude. And the refrain echoes older words.

teach.h: THOU ART GREAT, O LORD GOD.
teach.b: When King David hears a promise from God in Second Samuel, he answers: "Wherefore thou art great, O LORD God." A psalm says it its own way: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works!"
Heard that way, the hymn keeps a simple order: look at what's there, then say so. Christians of different churches sing it, in different languages, at weddings and funerals and on ordinary Sundays.
It started with a man walking home after a storm.

how: How Great Thou Art is sung by Christians of different churches, in congregations, at revival meetings, weddings and funerals, and it appears in hymnals in different languages.

games.q: you're walking home along a Swedish bay. a sudden storm has just passed: the air is clean, birds are singing, church bells ring across the water. what do you do?
o: hurry inside before the next one.
go home and write a poem: O great God.
complain about the weather in a letter.
games.why: the story goes that Carl Boberg went home and wrote O store Gud, O great God, which became How Great Thou Art.

practice: If you know How Great Thou Art, sing the first verse, quietly or out loud; if you don't, read the eighth Psalm's line slowly: when I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers.
Then look closely at one made thing, a leaf, a stone, the lines of your own palm. If you pray, let the hymn's title be your whole prayer; if not, let that one thing hold your attention.

orig.note: Hebrew: great — as in "Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised" in Psalm 48:1.
